title: Environment setup & your first Playwright project

parts.title: Environment setup & your first Playwright project

blocks.text:
# Week 1 - Day 2 - Fundamentals - Environment setup & your first Playwright project

Before you can write a test, your computer needs three things: Node.js, a code editor, and a
Playwright project. In this lesson, you install the first two and create the third.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | Installing the tools that Playwright needs, and creating your first Playwright project. |
| **Goals** | Check your Node.js version, set up VS Code, create a project with `npm init playwright@latest`, and recognize the files it creates. |
| **Prerequisites** | [Day 1 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d1/p2), and a computer on which you can install programs. |
| **Environment** | Your computer's terminal and VS Code, where you run each command in this lesson. |

## Step 1: Open a terminal

A **terminal** is a program in which you type commands for your computer to run. You type a
command, press Enter, and the result appears below it.

| Operating system | How to open a terminal |
|---|---|
| Windows | Open the Start menu, type **PowerShell**, and select **Windows PowerShell**. |
| macOS | Press Command and Space, type **Terminal**, and press Enter. |
| Linux | Open the application menu and select **Terminal**. |

## Step 2: Install Node.js

**Node.js** is a program that runs JavaScript and TypeScript code outside a web browser. Playwright
runs on Node.js. Installing Node.js also installs **npm**, a tool that downloads **packages**: code
that other people have written and shared, such as Playwright itself.

To check whether Node.js and npm are installed, run these two commands in the terminal:

```bash
node -v
npm -v
```

**Output**

```output
v22.12.0
10.9.0
```

**Explanation:** Each command prints a version number. Your numbers will be different, which is
expected. Playwright needs Node.js version 20 or later, so the first number must be 20 or higher.

If the terminal reports that `node` is not recognized, or on macOS and Linux
`command not found: node`, Node.js is not installed yet. Download the **LTS** version from
https://nodejs.org and install it. LTS stands for long-term support: the version that receives
updates for the longest time. Then close the terminal, open a new one, and run the two commands
again. A terminal that was open before the installation does not know about Node.js.

## Step 3: Install Visual Studio Code

**Visual Studio Code**, usually called **VS Code**, is a free code editor from Microsoft. A **code
editor** is a program for writing and editing code. Download it from https://code.visualstudio.com
and install it.

You use three features of VS Code throughout this course:

| Feature | How to use it | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Open Folder | Select **File**, then **Open Folder**, and choose your project folder. | VS Code then treats everything in that folder as one project. |
| Trust the folder | When VS Code asks whether you trust the authors of the files, select **Yes, I trust the authors**. | VS Code turns off some features in a folder until you trust it. |
| Integrated terminal | Select **View**, then **Terminal**. | This opens a terminal inside VS Code that already points at your project folder. |

## Step 4: Create your Playwright project

A **project** is a folder that contains your tests and the settings that Playwright needs to run
them. To create one:

1. Create an empty folder named `playwright-course`, for example in your Documents folder.
2. In VS Code, open the folder, and trust it when asked.
3. Open the integrated terminal, and run this command:

```bash
npm init playwright@latest
```

Before the questions, npm may first print `Need to install the following packages:`, the name of a
package, and `Ok to proceed? (y)`. Type `y` and press Enter.

The command then asks four questions. For the first, use the arrow keys to move to your answer and
press Enter. Each of the others shows a suggested answer in brackets: press Enter to accept it, or
type `y` or `n` and press Enter. Answer them as follows:

| Question | Your answer |
|---|---|
| Do you want to use TypeScript or JavaScript? | **TypeScript** |
| Where to put your end-to-end tests? | **tests**, the suggested answer |
| Add a GitHub Actions workflow? | **No**. **GitHub** is a website where teams share code, and **GitHub Actions** is its service for running tests on a server. This course does not need it. |
| Install Playwright browsers? | **Yes** |

On Linux, the command also asks whether to install the system packages that the browsers need.
Answer **Yes**.

**Output**

The last lines look similar to this:

```output
Inside that directory, you can run several commands:

  npx playwright test
    Runs the end-to-end tests.

We suggest that you begin by typing:

    npx playwright test

And check out the following files:
  - ./tests/example.spec.ts - Example end-to-end test
  - ./playwright.config.ts - Playwright Test configuration
```

**Explanation:** The command installs Playwright into your folder and downloads the three browsers
that it tests with. It then writes the files described in the next section. It can take a few
minutes, because the browsers are large downloads. The output suggests `npx playwright test`, which
you run in [Day 3 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d3/p2). **`npx`** comes with npm and runs a command
that a package provides, such as `playwright`.

> **Important:** **Run this command only in a new, empty folder.** In a folder that already
> contains a Playwright project, it can replace the existing configuration file.

## What the command creates

Your folder now contains these files and folders:

```text
playwright-course/
  node_modules/          the packages npm installed, including Playwright
  tests/
    example.spec.ts      an example test file that checks the Playwright website
  .gitignore             the list of files that Git should not save
  package.json           the list of packages that your project uses
  package-lock.json      the exact version of every installed package
  playwright.config.ts   the settings Playwright reads each time it runs your tests
```

You never edit `node_modules/` or `package-lock.json` by hand, because npm manages them for you.
**Git** is a tool that saves the history of a project's files, so that a team can share them, and
`.gitignore` lists what it must not save. [Implementation](/learn/w1/d2/p3) explains `.gitignore`
and how to organize your tests.

## A first look at the configuration file

`playwright.config.ts` is the **configuration file**: it holds the settings for every test run.
To open it, select it in the **Explorer** panel on the left of VS Code, which lists the files of
your project. Most of the file is comments. Text between `/*` and `*/` is a **block comment**: notes
for people to read, which the computer ignores, and the file uses them to describe each setting.
Without its comments, the main part looks like this:

```ts
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './tests',
  fullyParallel: true,
  reporter: 'html',
  use: {
    trace: 'on-first-retry',
  },
  projects: [
    { name: 'chromium', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } },
    { name: 'firefox', use: { ...devices['Desktop Firefox'] } },
    { name: 'webkit', use: { ...devices['Desktop Safari'] } },
  ],
});
```

Four settings are worth recognizing now:

| Setting | What it means |
|---|---|
| `testDir: './tests'` | Playwright looks for test files in the `tests` folder. |
| `reporter: 'html'` | After each run, Playwright creates a report that you open in a browser. |
| `baseURL` | The address that short page addresses start from. In a new project, its line starts with `//`, which makes it a comment, so it is not set. |
| `projects` | The browsers that each test runs in. Here, every test runs in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit. Each test runs once per browser, so three browsers take about three times as long as one. |

[Day 3 - Implementation](/learn/w1/d3/p3) explains every setting in the file.

## Best practices

- Always open your project folder in VS Code before you run a command, so that the command runs in
  the right place.
- Keep the answers suggested in this lesson. Later lessons assume a TypeScript project with its
  tests in the `tests` folder.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Opened the terminal before installing Node.js | `node` is not recognized, or `command not found: node` | Close the terminal and open a new one. If it is the terminal inside VS Code, close and reopen VS Code. |
| PowerShell does not allow scripts to run | `npm.ps1 cannot be loaded because running scripts is disabled on this system` | Run `Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned`, answer `Y`, and run your command again. |
| Answered **No** to installing the browsers | Later, `browserType.launch: Executable doesn't exist` | Run `npx playwright install` in your project folder. |
| Ran the command in the wrong folder | The files appear in an unexpected place | Open the correct folder in VS Code, and run the command again there. |
What does the command `npm init playwright@latest` do?

options: It runs every test in the current folder and shows the results.
It creates a Playwright project, installs Playwright, and downloads the browsers.
It updates Node.js and npm to the newest versions available.
checkpoint.explanation: The command sets up a new project in the current folder. It installs Playwright, downloads the Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit browsers, and writes files such as `playwright.config.ts` and an example test. It runs no tests itself.

blocks.text: In a new project, where does Playwright look for test files?

options: In the `node_modules` folder, where npm installed Playwright
In the folder that `testDir` names in the configuration file
In every folder that contains a `package.json` file on your computer
checkpoint.explanation: `testDir: './tests'` in `playwright.config.ts` tells Playwright to look in the `tests` folder. That is why the example test is in `tests/example.spec.ts`.

blocks.text: Weeks later, a test fails with `browserType.launch: Executable doesn't exist`. What is the most likely cause?

options: Node.js is too old for the installed version of Playwright.
The browsers were never downloaded when the project was created.
The configuration file has no `projects` entry for that browser at all.
checkpoint.explanation: Playwright and its browsers are separate downloads. If you answered No to installing the browsers, Playwright is installed but the browsers are missing. Running `npx playwright install` in your project folder downloads them.

blocks.text:
- **Node.js** runs your tests, and **npm** installs packages such as Playwright. `node -v` and `npm -v` show their versions, and Playwright needs Node.js 20 or later.
- **VS Code** is the editor you write tests in. Open your project folder in it, and use its integrated terminal.
- `npm init playwright@latest` creates a project in an empty folder. Answer TypeScript, tests, No, and Yes.
- `playwright.config.ts` holds the settings for every run. `testDir` tells Playwright where the tests are.
- Playwright and its browsers are separate downloads. `npx playwright install` downloads missing browsers.

## What's next

[Implementation](/learn/w1/d2/p3) shows how to organize the folders of a project as it grows, and
which files belong in `.gitignore`.

parts.title: Organizing a real project's folders and config

blocks.text:
# Week 1 - Day 2 - Implementation - Organizing a real project's folders and config

A new project keeps every test in one `tests` folder. As a project grows, that stops working well.
This lesson shows how teams organize test files into folders, how the configuration file finds
them, and which files to keep out of version control.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | Organizing test files into folders, and choosing which files to keep out of Git. |
| **Goals** | Explain what `testDir` and `testMatch` decide, and which entries belong in `.gitignore` and why. |
| **Prerequisites** | [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d2/p2), where you created your project and opened its configuration file. |
| **Environment** | The editor on the right for the example, and your own project's `playwright.config.ts` and `.gitignore` for the rest of the lesson. |

## Why one folder stops working

A real project soon has different kinds of tests: for example, tests of the web interface and
tests of an API. Different kinds of tests often need different setup. When all of them sit in one
folder, it becomes hard to run only one kind, such as only the API tests.

A common solution is to give each kind of test its own folder:

```text
tests/
  ui/
    login.spec.ts
    dashboard.spec.ts
  api/
    accounts.spec.ts
```

Group tests by what they have in common, such as the setup they need. Do not group them by the
order in which you wrote them.

## How Playwright finds test files

Two settings in `playwright.config.ts` decide which files Playwright runs:

| Setting | What it decides | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `testDir` | The folder where Playwright starts looking | `'./tests'` |
| `testMatch` | Which file names count as tests, inside that folder | `'**/*.spec.ts'` |

`testMatch` uses a **pattern**: a short description that matches many file names at once. In the
pattern `**/*.spec.ts`, the `**` means "in any folder", and `*.spec.ts` means "any file name that
ends in `.spec.ts`". A new project does not set `testMatch`, so Playwright uses its default
pattern, which matches every file whose name ends in `.spec.ts` or `.test.ts`, and the JavaScript
versions of those names.

The example below writes three configurations as plain data, so that you can compare them. It runs
in the editor on the right: select **Load into editor**, then select **Run**, and its result
appears in the **Console** tab below the editor. Every word in this code is explained in
[Day 5 - TypeScript](/learn/w1/d5/p1) and [Day 5 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2). For now, copy
it as written. It prints each configuration:

```ts
const newProject = { testDir: './tests' };
const uiOnly = { testDir: './tests', testMatch: 'ui/**/*.spec.ts' };
const uiAndApi = { testDir: './tests', testMatch: ['ui/**/*.spec.ts', 'api/**/*.spec.ts'] };

console.log('new project:', JSON.stringify(newProject));
console.log('UI only:    ', JSON.stringify(uiOnly));
console.log('UI and API: ', JSON.stringify(uiAndApi));
```

**Output**

```output
new project: {"testDir":"./tests"}
UI only:     {"testDir":"./tests","testMatch":"ui/**/*.spec.ts"}
UI and API:  {"testDir":"./tests","testMatch":["ui/**/*.spec.ts","api/**/*.spec.ts"]}
```

**Explanation:** `testDir` alone only says where to start looking. `testMatch` narrows the search
to the files you want. `JSON.stringify` turns each configuration into a line of text, so that
`console.log` can print it.

// Write a fourth configuration that runs only the files in tests/smoke,
// then print it with console.log and JSON.stringify.

variation.prompt: Add a fourth configuration that runs only the files in a folder named smoke, and print it in the same way. A smoke test is a quick test of the most important features, run first to check that the application works at all.

blocks.text:
## Keeping files out of version control

**Git** is a **version control** tool: it saves the history of the files in a project, so that you
can see what changed and share your work with a team. The **`.gitignore`** file lists the files and
folders that Git must not save.

`npm init playwright@latest` writes these entries into your project's `.gitignore`:

```text
node_modules/
/test-results/
/playwright-report/
/blob-report/
/playwright/.cache/
/playwright/.auth/
```

| Entry | What it contains | Why Git ignores it |
|---|---|---|
| `node_modules/` | The installed packages | npm can install them again from `package.json` at any time. |
| `test-results/` | Screenshots, videos, and traces from a run | Playwright writes them again on every run. |
| `playwright-report/` | The report of the last run | Playwright writes it again on every run. |
| `blob-report/` | Report pieces for combining runs from several computers | Playwright writes them again on every run. |
| `playwright/.cache/` | Temporary files that Playwright keeps between runs | Playwright recreates them when it needs them. |
| `playwright/.auth/` | Saved sign-in details, used by tests that start already signed in | They can contain passwords or other private data. |

> **Important:** **If a test run creates a file again each time, it does not belong in Git.**
> Private data, such as saved sign-in details, never belongs in Git either.

> **Note:** Your project is not in Git yet, and this course does not require it. The `.gitignore`
> file is already written, so it costs nothing now and is ready when a team adds Git.

## Best practices

- Give each kind of test its own folder, and group tests by the setup they share.
- Keep `testDir` and `testMatch` in the configuration file, so that every run finds the same tests.
- Add any file that a run creates again to `.gitignore`.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Saved `test-results/` or `playwright-report/` in Git | The project grows large, and every change includes report files | Add the folders to `.gitignore`, and ask a teammate who uses Git to remove the saved copies. |
| Put every kind of test in one folder | It is hard to run only one kind, because their files are mixed together | Give each kind its own folder, and use `testMatch` to select it. |
You move your tests into `tests/ui` and `tests/api`, and want to run only the UI tests. Which setting selects them?

options: `testDir`, because it lists every folder that Playwright should search for tests
`testMatch`, because it decides which file names inside `testDir` count as tests
`reporter`, because it decides which test results Playwright shows you after a run
checkpoint.explanation: `testDir` says where Playwright starts looking. `testMatch` decides which files count as tests once it is there, so a pattern such as `ui/**/*.spec.ts` selects only the UI tests. Naming a folder on the command line, as in `npx playwright test tests/ui`, runs it once, while `testMatch` decides which files count as tests on every run.

blocks.text: Which rule decides whether a file belongs in `.gitignore`?

options: If the file is too large to share easily, Git should ignore it.
If each test run creates it again, Git should ignore it.
If the file is not written in TypeScript, Git should ignore it.
checkpoint.explanation: `node_modules/` can be installed again from `package.json`, and `test-results/` and `playwright-report/` are written again on every run. Saving them in Git makes the project large, and fills every change with report files.

blocks.text:
- Give each kind of test its own folder, and group tests by the setup they share.
- `testDir` tells Playwright where to start looking. `testMatch` decides which files count as tests.
- A **pattern** such as `**/*.spec.ts` matches many file names at once.
- **Git** saves the history of a project. **If a run creates a file again each time, it does not belong in Git.**

## What's next

[Practice](/learn/w1/d2/p4) has you check your own setup and read your project's configuration file.
In [Day 3 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d3/p2), you run tests from the terminal.

# Week 1 - Day 2 - Practice - Environment setup

These three problems check the setup you completed in [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d2/p2). Each answer
is something you can find on your own computer or in your own project.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | Three problems that check your setup and your project's configuration file, from Beginner level to Advanced. |
| **Prerequisites** | [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d2/p2) and [Implementation](/learn/w1/d2/p3), and the project you created. |
| **Environment** | Your terminal and VS Code, where you find each answer, and the editor on the right, where you write it. |

## How to answer

Select **Start this in the editor** to open a template for a problem, and write your answer on the
lines that start with `//`. Select **Reveal solution** to compare it with a model answer.
[Day 1 - Practice](/learn/w1/d1/p4) explains how the problems work in more detail.

## When you are done

Your computer can now run Playwright, and you know the main parts of a project and its
configuration file. In [Day 3 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d3/p2), you run tests from the terminal.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** A record of the Node.js and npm versions on your computer.

**Where.** Run `node -v` and `npm -v` in your terminal, and write the two version numbers in the
editor, using the template.

**How you will know it worked.** You wrote down two version numbers from your own computer, and
the Node.js version is 20 or higher.

**What to build.** Answers to four questions about your project's configuration file. Open
`playwright.config.ts` in VS Code and answer from what you see in the file:

1. Which folder does `testDir` name?
2. Which browsers does `projects` list, not counting lines that start with `//`?
3. Which reporter does `reporter` name?
4. Is `baseURL` set, or does its line start with `//`?

**Where.** In the editor, using the template.

**How you will know it worked.** Each answer comes from your own `playwright.config.ts`, not from
the lesson.
problems.solution:
**A model answer**, for a project created with the answers from [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d2/p2):

> 1. **`testDir`** names `./tests`, the folder that holds `example.spec.ts`.
> 2. **`projects`** lists `chromium`, `firefox`, and `webkit`. The file also contains entries for mobile browsers, Microsoft Edge, and Google Chrome, but their lines start with `//`, so Playwright ignores them.
> 3. **`reporter`** names `html`, the report that you open in a browser after a run.
> 4. **`baseURL`** is not set. Its line starts with `//`, so it is a comment. You learn what `baseURL` does in [Day 3 - Implementation](/learn/w1/d3/p3).

**What makes a good answer** is that every answer comes from the file itself. A line that starts with `//` is a comment, so the setting on it has no effect. Reading a configuration file carefully is how you find out what a project really does.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** A short plan for a second project. Imagine that you are setting up a new
Playwright project for a team tomorrow. Decide these three things, and give a reason for each:

1. Would you keep one `tests` folder, or give each kind of test its own folder?
2. Would you run every test in all three browsers from the start, or begin with one?
3. Would you answer **Yes** to the GitHub Actions question this time?

**Where.** In the editor, using the template.

**How you will know it worked.** Each decision has a reason, not only a preference.
problems.solution:
**A model answer.** There is no single right plan, but each choice needs a reason.

> **Folders.** I would give each kind of test its own folder from the start, such as `tests/ui` and `tests/api`. Moving files later means changing the configuration, and every teammate has to learn the new layout.
>
> **Browsers.** I would begin with Chromium only. Running every test in three browsers takes three times as long, and early failures are usually mistakes in the tests, not differences between browsers. I would add Firefox and WebKit once the tests are stable.
>
> **GitHub Actions.** Yes. For a team, running the tests automatically on a server each time someone changes the code keeps the tests trustworthy.

**What makes a good answer** is a reason for each choice. The answer "Three browsers, because more is better" states a preference. The answer "Chromium first, because early failures are usually my own mistakes" states a reason.
